analysis.one_liner: Tightens ethics rules for the President, senior officials, and their businesses, including required tax disclosure and divestiture.
analysis.headline: The Restoring the Public Trust Act never received a committee vote or floor action; it sat in four House committees and subcommittees for two years and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have imposed a package of ethics rules on the executive branch: senior officials and their spouses would have to move conflicting business holdings into blind trusts, the President and Vice President would have to publish their tax returns, agencies would have to report any money they spend at the President's own businesses, and officials staying at properties they own would have to repay the government for security costs. It would also create a new crime for using public office for private gain, bar the President's family businesses from federal contracts, require the White House to publish visitor logs, and force the President to explain to Congress why Inspector General posts sit vacant.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently pay for government travel, security, and hotel stays at properties owned by federal officials; future voters, who would get to see presidential and vice-presidential tax returns; and watchdog agencies, whose Inspector General vacancies would have to be explained to Congress.

how_it_helps.text: The President, Vice President, and Cabinet-level officials would have to submit their last 10 years of income tax returns to the Federal Election Commission, which would make them public with personal identifiers redacted [S3].

If a protected official stays at a hotel or resort they own, they would have to reimburse the Treasury for the Secret Service and other government costs of that stay, ending taxpayer subsidy of officials' own businesses [S3].

Senior officials and their spouses would have to divest significant business holdings (anything where they are trustee, partner, officer, director, or a >10% shareholder) into a blind trust, with violations subject to court action by the Attorney General, states, or aggrieved persons [S3].

Using public office for private gain would become a federal crime punishable by up to one year, or up to five years if willful, applying to the President, Vice President, and senior White House and Senate-confirmed officials [S3].

The President, Vice President, their immediate family members, and their businesses would be barred from new federal contracts, leases, and grants while in office, and each agency would have to report its spending at the President's properties to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics [S3].
The White House would have to publish visitor logs, employee salaries, and financial disclosure forms on a searchable public website, updated on a set schedule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, senior political appointees, and their family businesses, which would face new divestiture duties, disclosure requirements, reimbursement obligations, and possible criminal liability; agencies and the White House would carry new reporting and publication workloads.
analysis.who_pays_short: The President, appointees, and their businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill targets a sitting president by name: its definitions and findings single out 'the Trump Organization,' President Trump's properties, and specific Trump administration officials, raising the fair-treatment objection that its rules are written for one person and one administration rather than as general law [S3].

The new criminal prohibition on using office for private gain is broad, covering endorsements and benefits to friends, relatives, and affiliated nonprofits, so conduct that today draws only an ethics reprimand could carry up to five years in prison under a willfulness standard [S3].

Requiring blind-trust divestiture by officials and their spouses could shrink the pool of wealthy people willing to serve in government, and the bill's reporting regime (agency spending reports, annual regulatory-conflict assessments, quarterly visitor-log updates) would add ongoing compliance costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and anti-corruption provisions address real problems documented in the bill's own findings, including taxpayer-funded security at the President's private resorts and undisclosed financial conflicts. But the bill's drafting undercuts its reach: by hard-coding 'the Trump Organization' and current officials into the definitions, it reads as a rebuke of one administration rather than a durable ethics framework, and a future Congress could just as easily strip such provisions out for the next president. The disclosure and reimbursement pieces are the strongest parts; the criminal and divestiture provisions are broad enough to invite selective enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees in early March 2019, and then nothing happened; no committee marked it up and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on January 22, 2019, with four original cosponsors [S1].
It was referred to four committees at once: Oversight and Reform, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and House Administration [S5].

On March 1 and March 4, 2019, portions were referred to the Oversight Subcommittee and the Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security Subcommittee; no markup, hearing vote, or floor action followed [S5].
The bill ended the Congress without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting federal officials and their business interests came out ahead: no new divestiture, tax-disclosure, reimbursement, or contract-ban duties ever took effect, and the existing ethics rules that allowed officials' travel and security costs at their own properties stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Senior officials and their family businesses

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to four committees

against.name: House Oversight and Reform, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and House Administration committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing vote, or floor recommendation; the bill remained in subcommittee referral from March 2019 until the Congress ended

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all five original sponsors and all four additional cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so the bill's support never extended past one party.

industries.industry: Trump family businesses (hotels, resorts, golf clubs)
industries.note: The bill would force reimbursement of government security and travel costs at properties the protected official owns, require agencies to report all their spending at these businesses, and bar the businesses from new federal contracts and funding while the President is in office. Under the status quo, federal spending continued flowing to these properties.

industries.industry: Senior federal officials with outside business interests
industries.note: Cabinet-level officials, noncareer senior executives, and White House senior staff would have to move conflicting holdings into blind trusts, and using the office for private gain would become a crime. These are the people whose financial conflicts the bill was written to reach.

industries.industry: Charter and private aviation operators serving government officials
industries.note: Federal funds could no longer pay for senior appointees' travel on private or chartered flights unless no commercial option existed and it was certified to Congress. High-profile cases of taxpayer-funded chartered travel, documented in the bill's findings, drove this provision.
